result:
On Saturday mornings, my father used to turn the kitchen clock to face the wall. He did this after breakfast, with the dishes still on the table and the last pancake cooling in the pan. He never announced it. One moment we lived in a house where it was nine fifteen; the next we lived in a house where a small round clock was studying the wallpaper. My mother wore a watch, of course. The oven had a green digital display. Nobody was being fooled. Still, something happened when he turned that clock around. We stopped asking what came next.

What came next, usually, was washing up. My sister washed and I dried, an arrangement based on the fact that she considered my washing inadequate and I considered her drying nonexistent. She would lift a plate from the water and hold it out without looking, confident that my hand would be there. For years I thought this was an ordinary way to do dishes. Only later, sharing apartments with people who set each object carefully in a rack, did I understand that we had worked out a little piece of choreography. Even now, handed a wet plate, I turn left.

Behind our house was a strip of land too narrow for a garden and too shady for grass. My father called it the orchard because a single pear tree grew there. The pears were terrible. They had a hard, gritty band around the core, and their skins went from green to brown without passing through any state you would willingly eat. Every autumn he picked them. Every autumn my mother set three in a bowl on the table. Visitors admired them. We accepted the compliments with the smooth, collective dishonesty of a family whose decorative fruit could break a tooth.

One Saturday, a branch came down. There had been no storm. We were inside arguing about whether a particular sheet of newspaper was old enough to put under a paint tin when we heard a crack, followed by the unmistakable sound of several dozen pears landing on the shed. Outside, the branch lay across the roof like an arm thrown over the back of a couch. A squirrel ran along it, stopped at the broken end, and looked down. For one absurd second we all waited for the squirrel to offer an assessment. Then my father went for the ladder.

The job took most of the morning. My father cut the branch into lengths while my sister steadied the ladder and I gathered pears in a bucket. My mother, who had objected to the pear tree on practical grounds for twenty years, stood in the doorway defending it against an accusation nobody had made. “It held on a long time,” she said. A neighbor came over with a better saw. Another brought coffee. By noon we had seven people in the yard, two ladders, three opinions about pruning, and enough wood to heat a room we did not actually have.

Among the fallen pears was one that had split cleanly in half. A wasp settled on it. I crouched to watch, mostly because somebody was about to suggest that I sweep the shed roof. The wasp worked at the flesh with such patient concentration that I began to feel we had judged the pears by an unnecessarily narrow standard. Here was a customer, after all. Here was genuine enthusiasm. When I told my mother, she said that if the wasp wanted the rest of them, it was welcome to bring a truck. She kept the split pear on the fence.

I remember that morning better than I remember my graduation. This seems unfair to everyone who rented a gown, drove through traffic, or sat on a folding chair waiting for my surname to arrive. I remember being happy at graduation. I remember a blister on my heel. But I cannot tell you what the sky looked like. On the morning the branch fell, the sky was white at the edges and blue directly overhead. The neighbor with the saw had shaving cream under one ear. My sister drank coffee from a measuring cup because we had run out of mugs.

For a while I tried to manufacture mornings like that. I invited friends over without an agenda, which meant that the absence of an agenda became the agenda, and I spent the afternoon anxiously checking whether everyone was being spontaneous. I bought pears from a market. They were delicious, which spoiled the effect. Eventually I understood that nobody in our yard had set out to make a memory. A branch had fallen. It needed moving. The coffee was not symbolic; the people holding the ladder wanted coffee. Whatever lasted had entered by a side door while we were carrying wood.

Last winter, my sister called while I was making supper. She had found the kitchen clock in a box of things our parents no longer wanted. Did I want it? I asked whether it worked. She said it lost eleven minutes a day. We agreed that this was a considerable professional failing in a clock, although perhaps consistent with its upbringing. A week later it arrived wrapped in an old dish towel. There was a pale rectangle on the back where a price sticker had been. I put in a battery and hung it beside the kitchen window, facing in.

It tells an increasingly improbable time. Yesterday I ate lunch at half past six. I could have it repaired, but its position is useful: from the stove, I can see the clock and, just beyond it, the apartment building opposite. Around dusk, a man there waters a row of plants with a blue jug. He takes each pot to the sink and lets it drain before returning it to the sill. I have no idea who he is. Sometimes, waiting for water to boil, I watch him finish. Then I salt the water, reach for the pasta, and make dinner.
